content.title: Response to Reviewer Yu1u
content.comment:
## Comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments.
### For Assumption 3: the gradient is bounded
Gradient clipping operation is often used to prevent the gradient explosion phenomenon in machine learning. Furthermore, assumption 3 (bounded gradient) is also commonly used in characterizing the convergence rate of federated learning [1-5]. Where [5] is a very classic work proposed by google for analyzing the convergence of adaptive optimizers in the presence of heterogeneous data for general nonconvex settings in federated learning. Thus, the gradient must be bounded in the experiment and we use the bounded gradient assumption in the theoretical derivation to correspond to the actual experiment on the real-world dataset. 

[1] Sun et al., "Decentralized federated averaging" TPAMI 2022.

[2] Yu et al., "Parallel restarted sgd with faster convergence and less communication: Demystifying why model averaging works for deep learning" AAAI 2019.

[3] Sun et al., "Stability and Generalization of Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent" AAAI 2019.

[4] Cheng et al., "Differentially Private Federated Learning with Local Regularization and Sparsification" CVPR 2022.

[5] Reddi et al., "Adaptive federated optimization" ICLR 2021.

However, theoretical research keeps pace with the times, and some new jobs have not required the gradient bounded assumption after this work [6], so our theoretical research should further follow and don't use the bounded gradient assumption. Where replacing all places that use the bounded gradient assumption with $||\nabla f(x^t)||^2$ with certain coefficients. Moreover, these techniques for analyzing convergence under unbounded gradient assumption are general, and we are working on an update of this part, as well as updating our analysis once we finish the detailed proof procedure. Thank you for this suggestion, which will make our theoretical contribution more solid.

[6] Nguyen et al. "SGD and Hogwild! convergence without the bounded gradients assumption." ICML 2018.

### The first decentralized FedAvg is ignored

We carefully read the paper: "Communication-Efficient Local Decentralized SGD Methods", and this paper is generally well-written and easy to follow.  We should first thank you for pointing out this paper. We will cite and give a comprehensive discussion of this work in the next version. Furthermore, we describe the connection and difference with this work as follows.
However, in the general classical federated learning algorithm, the client adopts multi-step local iterations by default due to the large communication overhead, such as FedAvg and other classic algorithms in related work of federated learning (FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedRobust, FedCM, FedAdam, FedDyn, FedSAM and so on). 

Therefore, due to the communication burden brought by frequent communication, we pay more attention to the decentralized federated learning scenario with multi-step local iterations. And this paper [1] "Decentralized federated averaging" is more consistent with our work. To the best of our knowledge, this work [1] is the first to consider both multiple local iterations and various communication networks, and they summarize the related works for decentralized training and decentralized federated learning, respectively. On the basis of this work, we further study the severe local model inconsistency problem in decentralized federated learning via SAM. Moreover, We will give a fair comparison for this work "Communication-Efficient Local Decentralized SGD Methods".

Furthermore, We also read many papers on decentralized training but do not summarize the related works in decentralized training due to space reasons. This part of the research work has been done for many years, such as some latest works [7-11] as follows:

[7] Zhu et al., "Topology-aware generalization of decentralized sgd" ICML 2022.

[8] Hashemi et al. "On the benefits of multiple gossip steps in communication-constrained decentralized optimization." TPDS 2022.

[9] Ye et al. "Deepca: Decentralized exact pca with linear convergence rate" JMLR 2021.

[10] Koloskova et al. "A unified theory of decentralized sgd with changing topology and local updates." ICML 2020.

[11] Ye et al. "Decentralized accelerated proximal gradient descent" NeurlPs 2020.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Yu1u
content.comment:
Comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments.
### Theoretical analysis is not difficult 
The analysis with multiple local iterations is different from that with one-step iteration. the technical difficulty is that local updates fail to be an unbiased gradient estimation after multiple local iterates, thereby merging the multiple local iterations is non-trivial.
The technical contribution is applying an optimization method SAM into a new setting while presenting a thorough theoretical analysis. This in itself is a nontrivial contribution. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to consider the model inconsistency problem in decentralized federated learning scenarios.
Moreover, our motivation is to adopt SAM to solve these unique problems in decentralized federated learning. In addition, we also experimentally explain the reason why the existing decentralized federated learning method (DFedAvg) performs worse than the centralized federated learning method (FedAvg) with the same setting as shown in Figure 2. Moreover, we solve the model inconsistency problem in decentralized federated learning and generate the model performance improvement compared with decentralized FedAvg.
Furthermore, we get an improved convergence rate compared with [1] in decentralized federated learning. To the best of our knowledge, our theoretical convergence rate is currently the fastest in the works of considering both multiple local iterations and various communication networks.
### Why does the MGS version even outperform FedSAM for CIFAR10
In decentralized federated learning, the local model inconsistency issue has a very serious impact on performance, especially on the complex dataset or in face of the sparse connectivity of the communication networks. SAM can make local model more consistent from the perspective of gradient perturbation. Based on SAM, MGS accelerates the aggregation process to further alleviate model inconsistency issues. Furthermore, decentralized federated learning is more communication-efficient than general federated learning.
Therefore, the MGS version outperforms FedSAM on a simpler dataset CIFAR10, and approaches FedSAM on a more complex dataset CIFAR-100. 
In general, the performance upper limitation of DFedSAM is consistent with FedSAM, after all, they just apply different optimizer algorithms to solve the same optimization problem. But for a simple dataset, DFedSAM will grow relatively faster and generate a better balance between communication and generalization. 
Some other evidence can also be found in the discussion on topology-aware performance in Section 5.3. On the sparser communication topology, the performance improvement of the MGS version is extremely significant. For instance, the performance is improved by 10.6% and 7.22% compared with the decentralized Fedavg in the ring and grid topology, respectively.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) has recently been shown to improve various aspects of deep learning. In this paper, the authors show empirically that SAM also helps to improve the performance in decentralized federated learning.

A main contribution of this paper is a theoretical analysis of their federated learning algorithms. However, this theory appears disconnected from the rest of the paper and it is unclear why it matters in practice (see weaknesses).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main weakness of the paper is the theory presented in Section 4. A lot of work is spent to derive a complicated and intimidating bound, and I am not convinced that this bound is important or matters in practice. For example, it is unclear if it matches any situations observed in practice. 

To improve the paper, some experiments could be added which demonstrate that this theory is correct or useful, as it is near impossible to confirm the math due to its complexity and presentation.  Just notice that for the considered deep learning applications, Assumption 1 and Assumption 3 may not hold.  Perhaps the authors could provide some "sanity checks" and show what happens on a simple federated linear regression problem. Does the theory work in that setting? Do the bounds / analysis simplify? 

If the theory Section 4 could explain some aspects of why SAM improves decentralized federated learning or give some guidance on the choice of parameters I would be convinced. But as of now, I don't see the point of including it. 

Minor typos (no influence on my rating):
- decebtralized -> decentralized
- Eq.2, SAM uses norm ||.||, not the squared norm. ||.||^2 is not a norm, so this sentence is technically wrong. Anyway, why write it with squared norm if simplified later?
- Commincation -> Communication
- typology -> topology
- desira ble -> desirable
- How are the weights W chosen? Perhaps a sentence can be added in the paragraph after Eq. (1) on how W is picked in practice.
- Section 3.2 is not very clearly written. In particular, does the neighbourhood N include the node itself, i.e., does Eq. (4) include also the weights of node i? In Eq. 5 why does it suddenly switch to "q" from "k"? The difference between Q and K needs to be explained, I suspect that the averaging happens every few inner iterations here? However, after reading Algorithm 1 in the appendix, these things became clear.
- Figure 5 (c) is very hard to read, especially for color-blind people. Perhaps the best result can be highlighted with a different line style or bold?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity/Quality:  see strengths/weaknesses. 

Novelty: The paper seems to be the first one to apply SAM to decentralized federated learning. However, the application is straightforward and applying an existing algorithm to an existing problem domain is of rather limited novelty. 

Reproducibility: the results seem possible to reproduce if the code is provided.

content.comment:
## Comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. 
### For Weaknesses: the extension of Generalized Federated Learning via Sharpness Aware Minimization 
Compared with the general federated learning scenario, decentralized federated learning can avoid the communication congestion problem and privacy leakage risk of the central server, so it has the advantages of higher communication efficiency and better privacy protection. However, decentralized federated learning also has some unique problems as follows:
1. Severe model inconsistency problem is caused by locality aggregation without a central server. This issue may cause the severe over-fitting problem in each client compared with general federated learning. 
2. federated learning scenarios also have a great impact on model training, especially on heterogeneous data or in face of the sparse connectivity of communication networks.
3. The analysis of the specific impact of communication topology on convergence is also very different from general federated learning scenarios.  
   

Therefore, our motivation is to adopt SAM to solve these unique problems in decentralized federated learning. In addition, we also experimentally explain the reason why the existing decentralized federated learning method (DFedAvg) performs worse than the centralized federated learning method (FedAvg) with the same setting as shown in Figure 2. Moreover, we solve the model inconsistency problem in decentralized federated learning and generate the model performance improvement compared with decentralized FedAvg. 
The technical contribution is applying an optimization method SAM into a new setting while presenting a thorough theoretical analysis. This in itself is a nontrivial contribution.

### For Weaknesses: How does the algorithm scale on the client size? 
In ablation study, we provide a figure on the small and large numbers of clients for studying the impact of different client sizes {50, 100, 150} in Figure 5 (b). When the client size is {50, 100, 150}, the training performance is {84.90%, 82.30%, 79.34%}, respectively. We find that the small client size has better training performance due to more samples in each client and the relationship between training performance and client size is approximately linear.
Moreover, this observation is also consistent with previous work [1], the performance will decrease when client size increases.

[1] Charles et al., "On large-cohort training for federated learning". NeurIps 2021.
### For Question: Are these two figures based on the real dataset in Figure 2?
Yes, we use the real-world dataset Fashion-MNIST [2] with the same setting.

[2] Xiao et al., "Fashion-mnist: a novel image dataset for benchmarking machine learning algorithms". arXiv 2017.

content.title: Response to Reviewer YESX
content.comment:
## Comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments.
### For the local maximization step in (2):
The normalized perturbation is used for seeking out model parameter values whose entire neighborhoods in a region of perturbation ratio $\rho$ have uniformly low training loss values. Moreover, The purpose of the local maximization step in (2) is to ensure that the training loss value is also low in the area where the perturbation radius is the largest. More details of the relevant principles can be found in the earliest paper on sharpness aware minimization [1], the link is https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01412.

[1] Foret et al., "Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization" ICLR 2021. 

In particular, we conduct some experiments on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 and Dirichlet 0.6 for a comparison between the current approach and the one replacing the normalized gradient perturbation with a random direction, where adding a random Gaussian noise with the same value $\rho=0.01$ of variance. The results show that the training performance with a random direction perturbation is severely worse than the current approach. Specifically, test accuracy is only 17.51% with a random direction, whereas current methods can achieve 60.47%  on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 after 200 communication rounds.

### For the x-axis in the plots:
Communication overhead is more concerned in federated learning scenarios, but in the distributed machine learning scenario, training performance vs. wallclock time is more concerned. In federation learning scenarios, the links between devices are often connected via low-bandwidth bandwidth. Thus a fair comparison is the training performance vs. communication overhead between various federated learning methods. Almost all work is comparing the performance under the same communication round, such as previous works [2-3]. Therefore, we take into account of communication round rather than gradient evaluation per local iteration in the plots. 

[2] Qu et al., "Generalized federated learning via sharpness aware minimization" ICML 2022.

[3] Caldarola et al., "Improving generalization in federated learning by seeking flat minima" CoRR 2022.

### For the selection on parameter $Q$:
We also find that the related work is provided in [4] for some theoretical guidance on how to select the parameter $Q$.

[4] Ye et al., "Decentralized accelerated proximal gradient descent" NeurlPs 2020.

In general, larger $Q$ can better solve the local consistency problem, but it also introduces additional communication cost. In the decentralized training setting, it is easier to obtain an optimal $Q$. However, in the decentralized federated setting, the upper bound of the convergence is more complicated because it can be related to heterogeneous parameter $\beta$, local interval $K$, etc., thus it is difficult to obtain an optimal $Q$ in the current bound. We only treat $Q$ as a hyperparameter in our experiments and conduct some experiments on different values of $1\leq Q\leq4$ under the various communication topologies, such as ring, grid, and exponential. Thus, we select the value from the set {1, 2, 3, 4}, thereby choosing $Q=4$.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper studies decentralized federated learning (DFL) and aims to improve inconsistency among local models and poor performance compared with its centralized counterpart (CFL). A key observation is that DFL induces a sharper loss landscape than CFL (e.g. in DFedAvg vs FedAvg). Based on this observation, the authors propose an algorithm that utilizes Sharpness-Aware Minimization in order to find flatter minima for DFL. The authors also present a theoretical analysis and show an improved convergence rates in the stochastic non-convex setting for the proposed algorithm. Finally, the paper empirically verifies that the proposed method can outperform existing DFL baselines.

The observation that DFL has sharper loss landscape is a very sound motivation for constructing a DFL algorithm that seeks flat minima, and I really like that. The authors did a great job in responding to the concerns raised by reviewers, and I find most of the concerns well-addressed. The only exception is some mistakes in the proofs raised by reviewer Yu1u around Eq.(20). Authors claimed their final result is correct, but admit problems in their derivation. Authors presented a modified derivation step in the rebuttal, and claimed that it has fixed the problem, but reviewer Yu1u believes the modification still has problems. Since problems around Eq.(20) can possibly lead to incorrect conclusions and/or arguments, unfortunately the submission can not be accepted. However, i do find the observations and the proposed approach quite interesting, and I do encourage authors to resubmit after revising their derivation.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: There is a flaw in the theory (around Eq 20), which can affect the conclusions and argument made by the paper.
